flawed_step: The assertion that normality passes to every subspace is false; it passes to closed subspaces, but not arbitrary ones.
counterexample: Let X=[0,ω₁]×[0,ω] with the product of the ordinal order topologies. X is compact Hausdorff, hence normal and T1. Remove the corner p=(ω₁,ω), and let Y=X\{p}. In Y define A={ω₁}×ω and B=ω₁×{ω}. These are disjoint closed subsets of Y, since each is the intersection with Y of a closed edge of X. Suppose U and V are open in Y with A⊆U and B⊆V. For every n<ω, openness near (ω₁,n) gives an ordinal α_n<ω₁ such that (α_n,ω₁]×{n}⊆U. The countable supremum α=sup_n α_n is still below ω₁. Let β=α+1. Then {β}×ω⊆U. Since (β,ω)∈B⊆V and β is an isolated successor ordinal, openness gives some N<ω with {β}×(N,ω]⊆V. Hence (β,N+1)∈U∩V. Thus A and B have no disjoint open neighborhoods, so Y is not normal.
assessment_summary: The deleted Tychonoff plank is an explicit nonnormal subspace of a compact Hausdorff—and therefore normal—space.
